text_blocks.snippet: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is treated through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when needed, prescription medications. The primary goal for most adults is to reach a blood pressure level of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
snippet_highlighted_words: heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when needed, prescription medications

text_blocks.snippet: Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with high blood pressure and can sometimes reduce or delay the need for medication:

list.snippet: DASH Eating Plan: Focus on a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Sodium Reduction: Lower salt intake (aiming for less than 2,000 mg or around 1,500 mg per day) to help drop blood pressure.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) and resistance training.
Weight Management: Lose weight or maintain a healthy weight if you are overweight or obese.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco products to protect your blood vessels.
Better Sleep: Aim for at least seven hours of quality sleep per night and screen for conditions like sleep apnea.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes alone are not enough, doctors prescribe blood pressure-lowering drugs. Treatment often starts with a single medication or a combination of two drugs (sometimes in a single pill):

list.snippet: ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., lisinopril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels (e.g., losartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to let vessels relax (e.g., amlodipine).

Thiazide Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body get rid of extra sodium and water.
(Note: For Black patients, guidelines often recommend thiazide diuretics or calcium channel blockers as preferred first-line choices).

text_blocks.snippet: If blood pressure remains uncontrolled (resistant hypertension) or if you have specific heart, kidney, or metabolic conditions, other classes of medications may be added:

list.snippet: Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and heart workload (often used if you have coronary artery disease or heart failure).
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRAs): Block aldosterone to reduce fluid and salt retention (such as spironolactone).
Central-Acting Agents or Vasodilators: Less common or specialized options for hard-to-treat blood pressure.

Newer Interventions: For stubborn or resistant cases, procedures like renal denervation (which targets kidney nerve activity) or the addition of GLP-1 medications (for patients with obesity/diabetes) may be evaluated by a specialist.

text_blocks.snippet: You can read more about prescription medications and guidance on the CDC High Blood Pressure Guide or review clinical treatment details via the NHLBI High Blood Pressure Treatment Page.
